Command: Do not eat leavened bread with the Passover on the afternoon of the fourteenth day
Summary: On the afternoon of the fourteenth day, when the Passover lamb is sacrificed, no leavened bread may be eaten with it.
Commandment: On the afternoon of the fourteenth day, eat no leavened bread with the Passover sacrifice.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule ties the leaven ban directly to the Passover sacrifice itself, not only to the seven-day feast. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).
Function: On the afternoon of the fourteenth day, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, no leavened bread might be eaten with it — a ceremonial law tying the leaven ban to the sacrifice itself. Its goal was to join the unleavened memorial directly to the Passover offering, not only to the seven-day feast. It did not address a particular evil; its work was remembrance and order, not restraint. The leaven was gone before the lamb was offered, and the sacrifice and the bread were one observance.
